question: A help center answers 50 000 simple factual questions a day from a 3 000-page knowledge base with per-customer documents. Which design fits best?
options: Send the whole knowledge base in every request
An agent that searches up to ten times per question
A fixed RAG pipeline with permission-aware hybrid search, a threshold and citations
Fine-tune a model on the knowledge base every night
explanation: High volume, simple questions, a corpus too big for the window and per-customer access all point to a cheap, predictable, permission-aware RAG pipeline.

question: An internal tool must answer "Which of our vendors renewed in 2025 and had a security incident afterwards?" across contracts and incident reports. What does agentic RAG add here?
options: Nothing: one search is always enough
The ability to decompose the question, search several sources, read the results and search again before answering
A larger embedding dimension
Automatic fine-tuning
explanation: Multi-hop, multi-source questions are where letting the model drive retrieval pays off, within budgets and stop rules.

question: A model accepts 1 million tokens. A team plans to put 900 000 tokens of policies in every request and drop retrieval. Which risk does "context rot" describe?
options: Performance on facts buried in very long inputs is less reliable than on short inputs, even within the window
The policies expire after a month
The model refuses long inputs
Long inputs are cheaper per token, which hides costs
explanation: A window that accepts the input does not use it uniformly. Studies show accuracy falling as input grows, especially for facts in the middle or with little lexical overlap; cost and latency also scale with input.

question: A small team has a 120-page product manual that changes twice a year and is visible to every user. What is a reasonable first design?
options: A vector database cluster with agentic retrieval
A knowledge graph
A custom-trained model
Include the whole manual in the prompt with prompt caching, and measure cost, latency and accuracy before adding retrieval
explanation: Small, stable, single-audience corpora are the case where long context is simplest. Retrieval can come later if the corpus or the costs grow.

question: Which control is essential before shipping agentic RAG?
options: A system prompt asking the agent to be efficient
A step and cost budget, a stop rule that allows "not found", and traces of every search
Removing the similarity threshold so the agent sees more
Letting the agent choose which users' documents to search
explanation: An agent loop can search forever on an unanswerable question. Budgets, stop rules and traces bound cost and make behavior inspectable; permissions stay inside the search tool.

question: Research comparing long-context models with RAG found long context can win on average quality when given enough compute. Why do production systems still use RAG?
options: Long-context models cannot cite sources
RAG is always more accurate
RAG is far cheaper and faster per request, supports per-user permissions and scales past any window; routing to long context only when needed captures much of the quality
Long context is not available through APIs
explanation: Quality is one axis. Cost, latency, access control and corpus growth usually decide, and hybrids such as routing combine both.
